**In Praise of Drifting**

The rain began at three in the afternoon, not with the theatrical crackle of a summer storm but as a slow, patient argument that the sky was having with the pavement. I was sitting in a café that had once been a butcher’s shop, eavesdropping on the leaky gutters and pretending to read a book I had already read twice. The book lay open on the table, its spine cracked, its margins filled with the hieroglyphs of earlier selves. I had come to that café because the wifi was weak, because the coffee was strong, and because I had decided, in a rare fit of self-respect, to spend an hour doing nothing that could be measured. The decision felt unlawful, like crossing a border without papers.

We live in a civilization that worships the arrow: goals, metrics, optimization, the relentless trajectory from point A to point B. Every hour is a budget line; every thought is a potential investment. There is an app for tracking sleep, an app for tracking water, an app for tracking the number of times we check our phones, which exists to shame us into checking our phones less, which we use while checking our phones. Efficiency has become the secular religion of the modern world, and its parishioners are never at rest. Idleness is a sin, boredom a failure of spirit, and the word “wandering” has been reduced to a metaphor for losing a tennis match.

But I have always been fond of the wrong turns. I suspect the map of a life is not a straight line but a tangle of loops, curls, and cul-de-sacs — a doodle that only makes sense when you lift the pen and step back. The people I admire most are not the ones who marched unerringly toward a single summit, but those who kept veering off the path to sniff the air, to paddle in the shallows, to ask a stranger about the weather. They understood that the destination is a rumor, and the journey is the only thing you can actually feel with your feet.

I was thinking of my own childhood walks home from school. The route was a simple triangle — three streets, two corners, one crossing guard who wore his fluorescent vest like a royal mantle. But I transformed it into an epic cartography. There was the alley behind the garages where moss grew like a green language on the bricks. There was the storm drain that sang after rain, a tinny, gurgling hymn. There was the fence with the loose board, behind which a plump cat named something unknowable lived its secret life. I would walk slowly, deliberately, trailing my fingers against walls, kicking stones that became planets. The stones were not “wasted time.” They were the raw material of an inner world. The twenty minutes of the walk were a cathedral of daydream, and I entered it every afternoon without a passport.

Somewhere along the way, I lost that cathedral. It wasn’t a single catastrophic loss, like a fire or a bankruptcy. It was more a gradual erosion, a hundred tiny surrenders to the logic of the arrow. The walks became commute. The commute became scrolling. The scrolling became a kind of restless meditation on all the things I wasn’t doing. The mind, once a meadow of loose associations, became a checklist. I began to measure my days in the currency of completion: emails sent, tasks crossed off, miles logged, hours of “deep work” banked. Even my leisure was managed, optimized, turned into a series of productivity playlists. I had become fluent in the language of the arrow, and I was proud of it.

And yet. And yet.

There is a reason that the greatest thinkers have often been the greatest wasters of time. Archimedes discovered the principle of buoyancy not in a laboratory but in a bath, where he had gone, presumably, to wash and not to solve a physics problem. Newton developed his theories of motion during a plague-enforced exile from Cambridge, when he was left alone with nothing but an orchard and his own wandering thoughts. Darwin took long daily walks around a path called the Sandwalk, and though he claimed the exercise was merely a pastime, he was known to pause for minutes at a time, staring at a beetle or into the abyss, letting the machinery of the mind grind in some secret, subterranean way. The stories may be apocryphal in detail, but they point to a deep truth: insight often arises not from concentrated effort but from its opposite. When we stop yanking at the thread, the knot sometimes loosens itself.

Modern cognitive science has a name for what happens during these idle moments. It calls it the default mode network, a vast constellation of brain regions that hums into activity when we are not focused on a task — when we are daydreaming, woolgathering, letting our minds slip the leash of intention. In this state, the brain does not rest. It churns. It connects distant memories, rehearses future scenarios, generates novel combinations, tells itself stories. It is, in many ways, the engine of creativity. But the default mode network is also fragile. It cannot compete with the dopamine-driven clamor of a smartphone. Every buzz, every ping, every compulsive swipe yanks the mind back into the spotlight of attention, where it must process incoming stimuli in real time, leaving no room for the slow, asynchronous alchemy of drift. We have filled the cathedral with slot machines, and we wonder why we no longer feel awe.

I am as guilty as anyone. I have stood in breathtaking landscapes and felt the urge to photograph them, not because I wanted to remember, but because I wanted to prove I was there — as if the experience itself were insufficient without a receipt. I have watched sunsets through a screen, their colors flattened into a rectangle of pixels, while my eyes paid homage to a flawed proxy. I have stayed up late reading arguments with strangers in comment sections, scrolling through the same handful of outrage-reactions, convinced that this was engagement with the world when it was only engagement with a mirror. The world is noisy, but the noisiest noise is the one inside my own pocket.

It was Pascal who wrote that all of humanity’s problems stem from man’s inability to sit quietly in a room alone. I used to read that as a counsel against distraction, a stern injunction to cultivate stillness. But I have begun to think that Pascal had it only half right. The problem is not merely an inability to sit quietly; it is an inability to sit quietly *without a purpose*. We have turned stillness itself into a performance, a box to check on the to-do list of wellness. We attend meditation retreats and track our “streaks” on apps, determined to achieve zero thoughts as efficiently as possible. But the mind is not a machine that should be switched off. It is a waterway. It wants to meander.

The meander is the shape of most living things. Rivers do not flow in straight lines; they curve, they braid, they pool, they carve oxbows that eventually cut themselves off and become silent crescents of slow water. Blood vessels branch like trees. Lightning forks. Even the path of a human life, if you trace it honestly, is not a line but a trail of breadcrumbs, some of them dropped on purpose, most of them scattered by chance. The English word “wander” comes from the Old English *wandrian*, which is related to the root meaning to turn, to wind, to change direction. It is kin to “windlass” and “winding.” To wander is to follow the way the world turns, not to impose a course upon it.

I decided, a few years ago, to rebuild my capacity for wandering. It was not easy. The anxiety that attends purposelessness is physical; it feels like a phantom limb of obligation. I would step out my front door with no destination, and immediately my mind would scream: *What are you doing? This is inefficient. Turn back. Check the news. Check your list.* It took weeks of patient practice to silence the accountant in my head. I learned to leave my phone at home, or at least in my pocket with the ringer off. I learned to make a rule: no maps, no clocks, no agenda. The first few walks were agonizing. I walked ten minutes in one direction, twenty in another. I stared at windows, at gardens, at the uncharted geography of neighborhood trees. I began to notice things: a door painted the impossible blue of a June sky; a forgotten tennis shoe dangling from a power line like a relic of a vanished god; an old man on a porch feeding a pigeon with the solemnity of a priest. The world had been there all along, patient as a houseplant, waiting for me to stop scrolling long enough to see it.

What happened next surprised me. The walks became less a exercise in discipline and more a form of nourishment. I would return home with my head full of half-formed sentences, with solutions to problems I had not consciously been pondering, with a strange, buoyant sadness that was not unpleasant. It was as though the mind had been given back its natural appetite. It had been starving, and I had been feeding it potato chips and energy drinks. I had forgotten that it also needed grapes and dark bread and water that tastes of limestone.

J.R.R. Tolkien once wrote that “not all those who wander are lost.” The line has been repeated so often that it has become a greeting-card motto, the sort of sentiment you see tattooed on forearms and printed on inspirational posters. But like most clichés, it has a genuine heart. The opposite of wandering is not arriving; it is being pinned. It is the condition of the pinned insect, the glassed exhibit, the cursor frozen on a desktop. To wander is to acknowledge that you do not know where you are going, and to be at peace with that ignorance. It is the beginning of humility. It is the recognition that the universe is larger than your plans, and that the best days are often the ones in which nothing was achieved and everything was received.

I have a friend who defines a successful walk as one in which she gets lost at least once. She used to live in Paris, and she would spend her Sundays in the outer arrondissements, deliberately taking the wrong métro line, walking until she no longer recognized the shopfronts, then finding her way back by sun and memory. The stories she tells from those walks are not about landmarks. They are about encounters: a baker who gave her a day-old croissant; a courtyard where an opera singer was practicing scales; a tiny museum dedicated to locks and keys, which she entered and never forgot. She did not accumulate these experiences by checking a list. She accumulated them by letting the city draft her itinerary.

There is a political dimension to this, too. The arrow culture is not merely personal; it is structural. Schools teach to standardized tests. Employers measure productivity in keystrokes and billable hours. Social media platforms monetize our attention. The economy wants us to be predictable, measurable, maximally efficient consumers of work and content. Wandering is a quiet rebellion against all that. It is a refusal to be optimized. It is a statement that the human soul retains the right to its own interiority, its own rhythms, its own time.

In recent years, I have come to see my walks not as a retreat from the world but as a more genuine form of engagement with it. When I used to rush, I experienced only a blur — a compressed montage of crosswalks and buildings, a surface without texture. When I wander, I encounter the world in its particularity. I notice that the barber on the corner has put up a string of Christmas lights in August. I notice that the lilac bushes outside the library are bursting with bees. I notice the sound of a distant train and the way it enters my daydream and becomes a scene involving a stranger who is running away from her own wedding, or a smuggler carrying a suitcase full of books. These stories are worthless in economic terms. No one will pay me for them. And yet they are the very texture of being alive.

The rain had stopped, though I did not notice at first. The café had emptied. The barista was wiping the counter with a cloth, moving in slow circular patterns. I closed my book, paid for my coffee, and stepped outside. The air was greener than before, rinsed and translucent. The pavement was covered with a mosaic of wet leaves. I could see a crack in the clouds, a seam of pale gold light, and I decided, quite deliberately, to follow it. I did not know where it would lead. The street curved left, then right, then opened into a small square I had never noticed in years of passing through the neighborhood. There was a fountain in the center, dry but beautiful, bordered by chipped stone benches. I sat down. I watched a pigeon take a bath in the bowl of water left by the rain. I thought about the book I had not read, the work I had not done, and the extraordinary luxury of being able to sit there, doing nothing, with no claim on my attention except the slow, swelling music of the ordinary.

There is an old word for this state, one that has been pushed to the margins of our vocabulary: “to while.” As in “to while away the hours.” It derives from the Old English *hwīl*, meaning a space of time, a pause, a respite. To while away time is not to kill it but to spend it generously, the way you might spend an afternoon with a beloved friend. It is time in which nothing is produced except the deepening of one’s acquaintance with the world. It is time that leaves no trace except the memory of having moved through the day with attention rather than acceleration.

I stayed on that bench until the light began to change from white to amber. Then I walked home by the long way, passing the barber’s shop, the library, the alley behind the garage. I did not take a single photograph. I did not check my phone. I counted nothing. I had a stupid, wonderful grin on my face, the kind that makes passersby look away. At some point, I crossed a street and was surprised by the color of the brick building in front of me — a warm terracotta that I had seen a hundred times but had never really seen. I know that sounds small. It was small. But smallness is the beginning of scale. From that one brick, I could have walked to the edge of the sea.

We are constantly being told that time is money. I have decided, after many years of believing it, to dissent. Time is not money. Money can be saved, spent, counted, hoarded, lost, and earned. But time does not move in the linear, ledger-like way of currency. It pools and eddies. It loops back on itself. It gives unexpected change. The only way to live with time is to stop trying to optimize it and start trying to inhabit it. And the way to inhabit it is to be present to it — to walk without a destination, to sit without a screen, to let the mind drift into the wild country where thoughts are not tasks and memories are not data.

The sun had set by the time I reached my front door. I stood on the porch for a moment, keys in hand, listening to the evening birds. Somewhere, far off, a dog barked. A car turned down a street and the sound of its engine faded like a held note. I had accomplished nothing that afternoon. I had not transformed the world. I had not been productive. And yet I felt a deep current of contentment, the kind that cannot be manufactured by achievement, only received as a gift. I unlocked the door, went inside, and wrote this down — not because I had to, but because the words were already there, blooming without permission, the way they always do when we finally give them room.

The arc of the world is toward order, or so we tell ourselves: from chaos to form, from scattered to systematized, from wanderer to citizen. But I wonder if the real arc is in the opposite direction. I wonder if we are born knowing how to wander — how to follow a bug with our eyes, how to drift off in the middle of a story, how to spend an hour turning a leaf over and over just because it is shaped like a boat — and then unlearn it, year by year, until we reach adulthood and believe that wandering is a four-letter word. I want to be a heretic. I want to reclaim the meander. I want to sit quietly in a room alone, and to wander loudly through the world, and to remember that every river writes its own name in the land as it goes. There is no destination that is not reached by turning. There is no thought that does not arrive by drifting.

So let the rain fall. Let the light change. Let the path curve away from the map. I intend to follow it — slowly, at last, without an outline — and see where it goes.
